title: Design YouTube (upload, transcoding, streaming)
scopeHtml: Scope: resumable upload, transcoding DAG, adaptive bitrate streaming, CDN, metadata. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
YouTube lets creators upload videos and lets anyone stream them smoothly on any device and network. Netflix, Hotstar and Vimeo share the same core: ingest a huge file, convert it into many formats, and deliver small pieces through a CDN. This note covers upload, transcoding and streaming.

Functional requirements

  • Upload a video (up to several GB), with title, description, thumbnail.
  • The system processes it into multiple resolutions and formats.
  • Watch a video with adaptive quality (480p on a weak network, 4K on a strong one); seek anywhere.
  • Basic metadata: views, likes, search by title (out of scope here but mentioned).

Non-functional requirements

  • Playback starts in under 2 s (time to first frame), very little rebuffering.
  • Uploads are resumable (mobile networks drop).
  • Highly available playback (99.99%); processing can lag minutes to hours.
  • Scale: 500 hours of video uploaded per minute (YouTube's publicly cited figure), 1B hours watched per day, strongly read-heavy.

Decision gravity. Choose adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS or MPEG-DASH) over serving one big MP4. It costs a transcoding pipeline and many stored copies but removes buffering for users on bad networks. This is a one-way door at the format level: players, DRM and CDN caching rules all depend on it. Netflix and YouTube both use it.

Everyday analogy. A bakery that bakes one loaf, then slices it into thin, medium and thick slices so every customer can take what they can chew.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing to stream a single file from your app server.
  • Forgetting resumable uploads.
  • Not separating the upload/processing path from the (much bigger) playback path.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/videos                      // step 1: create metadata, get an upload session
{ "title": "My trip", "description": "...", "sizeBytes": 2147483648, "contentType": "video/mp4" }
201 { "videoId": "v_8Hq2", "uploadUrl": "https://up.yt.com/u/sess_91", "chunkSize": 8388608 }
PUT https://up.yt.com/u/sess_91     // step 2: upload chunks, resumable
Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/2147483648
308 Resume Incomplete   Range: bytes=0-8388607
...
200 OK                   (last chunk)  { "videoId": "v_8Hq2", "status": "PROCESSING" }

HEAD/PUT with Content-Range: bytes */2147483648   -> returns how many bytes the server has (resume)
GET /v1/videos/v_8Hq2
200 { "videoId":"v_8Hq2", "status":"READY", "title":"My trip", "durationSec": 612,
      "manifestUrl": "https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/master.m3u8",
      "thumbnailUrl": "https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/thumb.jpg", "views": 15234 }
GET https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/master.m3u8     // HLS master playlist
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8

GET https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/1080p/seg_00042.ts    // 4-6 s segment, cacheable forever

Status moves UPLOADING -> PROCESSING -> READY | FAILED. This resumable protocol resembles the Google Cloud Storage resumable upload and tus.io; confirm exact header details in their docs.

Industry example. YouTube Data API uses resumable uploads; Netflix and Twitch publish HLS/DASH manifests.

Everyday analogy. A courier who gives you a tracking number, accepts the parcel in several trips, and tells you where he stopped if the van breaks down.

Common interview traps.

  • Uploading through the app server instead of directly to object storage using a pre-signed/session URL.
  • One giant PUT with no resume.
  • Serving video bytes through the API gateway.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 500 hours uploaded per minute, average source 1080p at 8 Mbps, 1B hours watched per day.

Quantity Calculation Result
Upload per day 500 h x 60 x 24 = 720,000 h/day 720k hours of video
Raw size 8 Mbps = 1 MB/s = 3.6 GB/hour; x 720k ~2.6 PB / day raw
Encoded ladder 144p..4K ladder totals ~ 1.5-2x the source size ~4-5 PB / day stored (before dedupe/cold tiering)
Upload bandwidth 2.6 PB / 86,400 s ~30 GB/s ingest = 240 Gbit/s
Transcode work 1 CPU-core encodes 1080p at ~0.5-1x realtime; a ladder ~5x work 720k h x 5 / 24 / 0.75 = ~200k cores continuously (hardware encoders reduce this a lot)
Playback bandwidth 1B hours x 3.6 GB (at avg 4 Mbps = 1.8 GB/h) = 1.8 EB/day ~21 TB/s average, ~100+ Tbit/s globally
Segment request rate 6 s segments, ~170M concurrent viewers ~28M segment requests/s

Takeaways: ingest and transcode are big but bounded; playback egress dwarfs everything and is why CDNs and ISP-embedded caches (Google Global Cache, Netflix Open Connect) exist.

Industry example. Netflix's Open Connect puts appliances inside ISPs; most of its traffic is served without leaving the ISP's network.

Everyday analogy. Making the bread is a night job for a few bakers; delivering it to a billion breakfast tables is the real logistics problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up bits and bytes (Mbps vs MB/s).
  • Skipping egress, the largest cost line.
  • Not saying that most videos are rarely watched (long tail), so cold storage tiers pay off.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components:

  • Upload service: issues resumable session URLs; chunks go straight to object storage (S3/GCS), multipart upload with 8 MB parts.
  • Metadata DB: Vitess/MySQL (YouTube used MySQL with Vitess) or Spanner/DynamoDB; video id, owner, status, rendition list.
  • Queue: Kafka/SQS; one message per video per task.
  • Transcoding workers: stateless pool using FFmpeg or hardware encoders; run as a DAG of tasks.
  • Processed store: object storage with segments plus manifests.
  • CDN: edge caches, then regional/origin shield, then origin.
  • Player: reads the manifest, picks a rendition by measured throughput.

Decision gravity: direct-to-storage upload. App servers stay light (they only mint URLs and track state). Alternative: proxy bytes through your servers; costs CPU, bandwidth and breaks at scale. Reversible.

Decision gravity: split video into segments (GOP-aligned 2-6 s chunks). It enables parallel transcoding, adaptive switching and CDN caching of small objects. A one-way door in practice since players and caches key on segment layout.

Industry examples. YouTube's published architecture (Vitess, Borg, Colossus) and Netflix's pipeline (the "Cosmos" platform and per-title encoding) follow this split.

Everyday analogy. A film lab: negatives come in through a loading dock, get duplicated in several sizes in the back, and finished prints go to local cinemas, not the lab.

Common interview traps.

  • A single monolithic transcode job per video (slow and not restartable).
  • Making the viewer wait until all renditions finish (publish lowest rendition first).
  • Treating the DB as the thing that stores video bytes.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Resumable, chunked upload

The session stores {videoId, totalSize, receivedBytes, uploadId} in Redis/DB with a 7-day TTL. Chunk 8 MB: smaller means more requests, larger means more resend on failure. S3 multipart allows up to 10,000 parts, 5 MB to 5 GB each; verify each part's checksum (MD5/CRC32C) and assemble on completion. Abandoned uploads are cleaned by a lifecycle rule after 7 days. Decision: chunk size is reversible per session.

Transcoding pipeline as a DAG

Steps: validate (reject corrupt files, virus/policy scan), split at keyframes, encode each chunk in parallel across hundreds of workers, then package into HLS/DASH segments with H.264 (universal), VP9/AV1 (smaller, slower), and AAC/Opus audio. A 10-minute video can finish in under a minute when split into 100 chunks. Idempotent tasks keyed by (videoId, rendition, chunk) so retries are safe. Priority queues: popular creators or livestream VODs first. Netflix uses per-title/per-shot encoding to pick the best bitrate ladder for each title, saving 20%+ bandwidth by their own reports.

Decision gravity: which codecs? H.264 everywhere, AV1 for popular videos only (encode cost is high but egress savings repay it when a video gets millions of views). This is reversible: you can add renditions later, though storing both costs space.

Adaptive bitrate streaming

The manifest lists renditions; the player downloads segment N at the quality its recent throughput supports (buffer-based and throughput-based algorithms), switching at segment boundaries. Typical ladder:

rendition  resolution  video bitrate
144p       256x144     0.1 Mbps
360p       640x360     0.8 Mbps
720p       1280x720    2.5 Mbps
1080p      1920x1080   5 Mbps
4K         3840x2160   16 Mbps

Segments are immutable and named by content, so the CDN can cache them for a year (Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable). Manifests for finished videos are cacheable too; live manifests need a 2-6 s TTL.

CDN strategy and the long tail

Popular 5% of videos produce most of the traffic: keep them at the edge. Long-tail videos fall through to regional caches or origin. Pre-position (push) new releases from popular channels. Hit ratio target above 95% at the edge; each 1% miss at 100 Tbit/s is still 1 Tbit/s hitting regional tiers. Cold content (no views in 90 days) moves to cheaper storage classes (S3 Infrequent Access/Glacier-like tiers), keeping only the lowest renditions hot and re-transcoding on demand.

Metadata, views and thumbnails

Metadata reads are cached (Redis, TTL 5 min). View counts: do not do UPDATE views = views + 1 per play. Batch increments through Kafka and aggregate every few seconds; show approximate counts (YouTube historically froze at "301 views" while validating). Thumbnails: extract a few frames, store as small JPEGs/WebP on the CDN.

Start-up latency and seek

Start with the lowest rendition for the first 1-2 segments then step up. Seek works by jumping to the segment containing the timestamp (index from the playlist). Smaller first segment (2 s) reduces time to first frame. Pre-connect TLS/DNS to the CDN.

Failure handling and DRM

Worker dies: queue visibility timeout re-delivers the task. Poison video: after 3 failures mark FAILED and notify the creator. DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady) is added at packaging with encrypted segments (CENC) and a license server; it only matters for premium content.

Production incident patterns. (1) A viral video's segments are cold in a new region: origin gets a thundering herd; fix with request coalescing at the origin shield. Metric: origin egress and cache hit ratio. (2) Transcoding queue backs up after a big upload wave: watch queue age, autoscale on it, and prioritise short videos. (3) Rebuffer ratio rising: track client-reported rebuffer %, per ISP.

Industry examples. YouTube (Vitess, Google Global Cache), Netflix (Open Connect, per-title encoding), Twitch (HLS with 2 s segments for lower latency).

Everyday analogy. A newspaper printing plant: the master page is cut into sections printed in parallel and trucked to local depots before breakfast.

Common interview traps.

  • A single transcoder queue with no parallelism within a video.
  • Updating view counts synchronously in the SQL row.
  • Ignoring the cache-hit-ratio math at CDN scale.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Separation of upload, processing and playback paths, and why each scales differently.
  • Direct-to-object-store resumable uploads.
  • Chunked parallel transcoding and an adaptive bitrate ladder (HLS/DASH).
  • CDN hierarchy, hit-ratio reasoning, cold-storage tiering.
  • Numbers: petabytes per day, egress in Tbit/s, cores for transcoding.
  • Trade-offs: codec choice vs encode cost, segment length vs latency, eventual counts.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Upload straight to object storage with resumable chunked sessions; app servers handle metadata only.
  • Transcode asynchronously: split into GOP chunks, encode in parallel into a ladder, package as HLS/DASH.
  • Players adapt quality per segment; segments are immutable and cached for a year on the CDN.
  • Egress, not storage or compute, is the dominant cost; edge caches and ISP appliances fix it.
  • Metadata in a sharded SQL or KV store with cache; counts via batched async aggregation.
  • Retries are safe because tasks are idempotent; poison videos go to FAILED.
  • Hard-to-change choices: segment layout, manifest format, DB sharding key.
